objectives: Classify common bacterial skin infection and screen for systemic spread.
Choose between local care only vs added oral antibiotics based on severity signs.
Provide hygiene counseling and follow-up instructions that reduce recurrence.
takeaways: Honey-colored crusted sores suggest impetigo; warmth and extension suggest deeper infection risk.
Fever, rapid spread, severe pain, or systemic illness raise urgency for broader treatment/referral.
Daily cleaning, hand hygiene, and early review are part of effective skin infection care.
learnCaseOverrides.blurb: A child with spreading crusted skin sores needs careful severity assessment and practical treatment planning.

sections.title: Chief complaint
sections.text: Crusted skin sores on legs, now spreading

sections.title: Caregiver note
sections.text: Lesions started as small blisters and became yellow crusts. One area is now tender.

coach.title: Ruth is uncomfortable but alert
coach.body: Your goal is to identify whether this is localized impetigo or a more serious spreading infection.

sections.title: Skin exam
sections.text: Multiple honey-crusted lesions on lower legs; one surrounding area mildly warm and erythematous, no abscess.

coach.title: What is the best working diagnosis?
coach.body: Use lesion pattern and systemic status.

options.text: Impetigo/skin bacterial infection with limited spread, currently stable
Fungal rash only, no bacterial component
No infection because fever is not high

question.right: Correct. Classic crusted lesions with mild local spread fit bacterial skin infection; no severe systemic signs are present now.
question.wrong: Lesion morphology matters. Dismissing infection because fever is modest can delay proper treatment.

sections.title: Treatment plan
sections.drug: Local wound care + consider oral antibiotic for spreading lesions
sections.detail: Daily cleansing, topical therapy, and oral therapy if cellulitic extension is present

sections.title: Escalate urgently if
sections.reveal_note: Caregiver understands hygiene and review timing.

coach.title: What is the best practical HC III approach?
coach.body: Select the option that balances treatment and stewardship.

options.text: Start local cleansing/treatment and add oral antibiotic when signs of spreading bacterial infection are present
Use steroids only to reduce redness quickly
No treatment; wait until lesions become painful
Give injectable antibiotics for every impetigo case

question.right: Correct. This approach treats likely bacterial infection while reserving escalation for worsening signs.
question.wrong: Either undertreatment or routine overtreatment can both harm care quality. Severity-guided treatment is key.

sections.title: Case outcome
sections.text: You managed likely impetigo/skin infection with appropriate severity-based treatment and hygiene counseling.
sections.emphasis: Lesion pattern plus systemic review guided safe prescribing.

coach.title: Key teaching points
coach.body: Child skin infections are common at HC III. Good outcomes rely on lesion assessment, practical hygiene education, and clear criteria for return or escalation.
